drawdown_context: Caleres is a two-segment footwear company: Famous Footwear (846-store family value-branded retail) plus Brand Portfolio (Sam Edelman, Naturalizer, Allen Edmonds, Vionic, Dr. Scholl's, Franco Sarto wholesale + DTC). FY24 (ended Feb 1, 2025) consolidated net sales declined -3.4% to $2.72B, operating earnings -22.9%, and diluted EPS dropped -35.6% to $3.09 from $4.80. Drawdown into 2025-05-15 reflects mall-anchor traffic erosion, sequential Q4 deterioration after a +2.5% Q3 Famous Footwear comp, leveraging up to fund a $105M Stuart Weitzman acquisition while continuing $65M of buybacks, and tariff overhang on $454.9M of China+Vietnam sourcing (~92% of total).

rfm_tuples.R: Famous Footwear comparable sales % change (1.3)% [FY24] vs (6.3)% [FY23]. Q3 FY24 10-Q (filed Dec 11, 2024) reported Famous Footwear Q3 standalone comp of +2.5% with YTD (39-week) comp of -0.9%. The FY24 full-year (-1.3)% is therefore arithmetically implied by a Q4 (Nov 3, 2024 - Feb 1, 2025) standalone comp of roughly -2.5% to -3% - a sharp reversal of the Q3 trend management was highlighting going into the holiday quarter.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B claim_evolution between FY24 10-K (Apr 1, 2025) and pre-cutoff Q3 10-Q (Dec 11, 2024). The Q3 10-Q narrative anchored on the 'returned to positive comp' Q3 print as evidence the strategy was working. Compute implied Q4 comp from FY-vs-YTD differential to test whether the FY-level (-1.3)% framing is masking a holiday-quarter collapse.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Q3 FY24 standalone Famous Footwear comp = +2.5%. 39-week YTD comp = -0.9%. FY24 full-year comp = -1.3%. Implied Q4 standalone comp = ~-2.5%, a ~5pp sequential deterioration from Q3. Management never breaks out the Q4 standalone comp in the 10-K MD&A.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The Q3 'returned to positive comp' narrative did not survive the holiday quarter - Q4 standalone comp reversed roughly 5pp into negative territory and management never breaks out the Q4 standalone comp in the 10-K MD&A. Mode-B reconstruction from claim_evolution forces the disclosure into the open. Classic late-cycle retail forensic tell.

rfm_tuples.R: In February 2025, we signed a definitive agreement to acquire Stuart Weitzman from Tapestry, Inc. for $105 million, subject to customary adjustments. The acquisition, expected to close summer 2025, will be funded through our revolving credit agreement. Risk factors flag potential write-offs of goodwill or intangible assets.
rfm_tuples.f: Capital allocation sanity check: $105M debt-financed acquisition layered on top of already-leveraged balance sheet (revolver $219.5M at FY-end, +$37.5M YoY) during a year of -22.9% operating earnings decline. Mode-B: test whether management is acquiring at the cycle bottom using debt because operating cash flow no longer supports both buybacks AND M&A.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Stuart Weitzman $105M, 100% debt-funded via revolver. Revolver already $219.5M (+20.6% YoY). Summer 2025 close pushes utilization toward $325M against $500M facility and $272.3M availability. Simultaneously executing $65M buyback + $9.7M dividends. Operating cash flow $104.6M (-47.7% YoY). Buyback + dividend + acquisition = ~$180M of capital uses vs $104.6M of operating cash generation.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Layering a debt-funded $105M acquisition on top of buybacks-into-trough while operating cash flow has been cut nearly in half is the textbook 'lever up at the wrong end of the cycle' pattern. Stuart Weitzman is a distressed-seller transaction (Tapestry off-loading). Management's own risk-factor language flags goodwill-writedown probability. Combined with Q4 comp cliff and 92% China+Vietnam sourcing exposure, this is leveraging into margin-compression.

rfm_tuples.R: Country ($ millions): China $244.7, Vietnam $210.2, Cambodia $21.4, India $12.9, Other $5.2, Total $494.4. 'The United States administration recently announced tariffs on products manufactured in several jurisdictions, including China, Canada and Mexico.' 'We believe we are well-positioned to manage additional tariffs through a combination of factory negotiations, selective price increases and modest gross margin pressure.'
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: derive the implied tariff hit. The 10-K discloses country mix and a qualitative 'well-positioned' claim but does NOT quantify the dollar-impact range. Compute implied COGS exposure: China = 49.5% of sourcing; China+Vietnam = $454.9M = 92%. Test whether 'modest gross margin pressure' is plausible against a footwear retailer with -1.3% comp.
rfm_tuples.M_value: China $244.7M (49.5%); China+Vietnam $454.9M (92%). 25% incremental China tariff = ~$61M COGS pressure on $149.9M operating earnings base - ~40% hit absent full pass-through. Wholesale customers (department stores) have limited price-elasticity headroom in -1.3% comp environment. NO scenario disclosure or sensitivity table in 10-K.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: 92% of CAL's sourcing is in the two countries most exposed to the tariff regime, and management uses the qualitative 'modest' descriptor without quantification, sensitivity analysis, or pass-through math. Reasonable scenario implies 20-40% of operating earnings at risk. Mode-B disclosure-quality failure: inputs are in the filing but synthesis is absent. Same 'well-positioned' framing was used during 2018-2019 China tariffs where pass-through was incomplete.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Failure to meet our debt covenants under the Credit Agreement may require the Company to seek waivers or amendments.' 'We were in compliance with all covenants and restrictions under the Credit Agreement as of February 1, 2025.' 'The Fourth Amended and Restated Credit Agreement matures on October 5, 2026, in an aggregate amount of up to $500.0 million.' 'On April 27, 2023, the Company entered into a Sixth Amendment to Fourth Amended and Restated Credit Agreement.'
rfm_tuples.f: Capital structure / refinancing wall check. Credit Agreement matures Oct 5, 2026 - 17 months past cutoff. Stuart Weitzman closes summer 2025 and pushes utilization. Six amendments to the Fourth Amended and Restated agreement indicate a long history of bank-syndicate renegotiation. Mode-B: covenant headroom + maturity wall against deteriorating earnings.
rfm_tuples.M_value: $500M facility, $219.5M drawn + $8.2M LCs = $227.7M utilization (45.5%); $272.3M availability. Stuart Weitzman draw + working capital seasonality pushes utilization to 65-70%. Maturity Oct 5, 2026 (17 months post-cutoff). 'Fourth Amended and Restated' + Sixth Amendment = 6+ rounds of renegotiation. Springing FCCR covenant of 1.25x triggers if availability falls below greater of $40M / 10% of Loan Cap for 30 days.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Technically in compliance with $272M availability - not a near-term liquidity crisis. But 17-month refinancing wall, imminent Stuart Weitzman draw, 47.7% YoY collapse in operating cash flow, and springing FCCR covenant create a setup where FY25 negotiation with bank syndicate will be from a materially weaker position than the 10-K narrative suggests. The 'Sixth Amendment' history evidences that the lender group regularly extracts pricing/covenant concessions.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Our borrowings under the revolving credit agreement increased $37.5 million to $219.5 million at the end of 2024, compared to $182.0 million at the end of last year. We used our revolving credit facility to repurchase $65.5 million of shares of our common stock under our share repurchase program.' 'Subsequent to our 2024 year-end, the Company has repurchased 150,000 shares at an aggregate price of $2.6 million.' 'During 2025, we will continue to evaluate our capital allocation priorities in light of business performance and market conditions.'
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B capital allocation tell: explicit disclosure that revolver borrowings funded the buyback. Test asymmetric pricing (buyback price vs current stock price) and proximity to insider activity / Form 4 cluster.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Buyback: $65.0M FY24 + $2.6M post-FY-end = $67.6M total, explicitly revolver-funded. Form 4 activity pre-cutoff clustered Mar 19, Mar 26, Mar 31, May 6 2025 - around 10-K filing window (Apr 1, 2025) and post-FY-end equity-grant cycle. Post-FY-end buyback rate (150K shares at $17.33/share) is dramatically slower than FY24 run-rate.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Management explicitly funded $65.5M of buyback through revolver draws while operating cash flow collapsed -47.7% YoY - a classic 'borrowed buyback.' Post-FY-end pace dropped to ~$2.6M (only 150K shares), and the 'continue to evaluate' language softens the prior commitment. Classic capital-allocation-tell: borrowed buybacks plus quiet hedging-back when the cycle turns.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Customer concentration and other trends in customer behavior may lead to a reduction in or loss of sales. Our wholesale customers include e-commerce retailers, national chains, department stores, independent retailers and mass merchandisers. Several of our customers operate multiple department store divisions.' The 10-K does NOT quantify any individual customer as 10%+ of revenue and does NOT name the top-3 wholesale customers.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: A wholesale-led Brand Portfolio segment ($1.226B FY24 net sales) selling to department stores and off-price MUST have meaningful customer concentration. ASC 280 / Reg S-K Item 101(c) requires disclosure of any customer >10%. Test against edgar_fts for counterparty disclosure mirror.
rfm_tuples.M_value: CAL's 10-K provides ZERO quantitative customer-concentration disclosure: no '10% customer' table, no named top-3 wholesale partners, no department-store-vs-mass-merchant mix. Risk-factor language is generic boilerplate. Counterparty edgar_fts queries against DDS, KSS, M, JWN, BURL, ROST, TJX for 'Sam Edelman / Naturalizer / Vionic / Allen Edmonds / Caleres' mentions - department stores rarely disclose vendor-level concentration, so the absence of CAL's affirmative disclosure when ~45% of revenue is wholesale to a stressed channel is itself the signal.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The disclosure gap is the finding. CAL has $1.226B of wholesale revenue (45% of total) flowing through a department-store channel in secular decline. The absence of any quantitative top-customer disclosure when this channel is the single largest forward risk to Brand Portfolio is a Mode-B disclosure-quality failure. Investors cannot size the exposure. Sector pattern: wholesale vendors with undisclosed top-customer concentration take the hardest negative surprises when downstream retailers file.

rfm_tuples.R: '/s/ Ernst & Young LLP We have served as the Company s auditor since 1917.' Critical Audit Matter: 'Inventory Markdown Reserves ... Auditing the Company s Brand Portfolio markdown reserves was complex and involved a high degree of subjectivity, as it included assessing the significant assumptions, including forecasted sales prices and demand.'
rfm_tuples.f: Auditor history + critical audit matter analysis. EY since 1917 is one of the longest auditor tenures in public markets - extremely low rotation risk but also low independence-signal value. The CAM (Brand Portfolio markdown reserves) is the area most impacted by Q4 comp deterioration and pending tariffs. Mode-B: test whether the CAM signals embedded reserve risk.
rfm_tuples.M_value: EY tenure since 1917 (108 years) - no auditor change risk. Unqualified opinion. Sole CAM = Brand Portfolio Inventory Markdown Reserves. Inventories $565.2M total, finished goods $550.2M, markdown reserve only $17.7M (3.2% of finished goods). Brand Portfolio uses 'permanent price reduction to clear slower-moving inventory' - so reserve % understates actual markdown depth realized through gross margin.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: EY surfacing markdown reserves as the SOLE CAM is meaningful in a year where comp turned negative again, tariffs on 92% of sourcing are imminent, and Brand Portfolio finished goods are $550M with only a 3.2% reserve. The CAM is the auditor's flag that reserve adequacy depends on management forecasts that may not survive Q1/Q2 FY25 sell-through. Combined with the Q4 comp cliff and buyback-funded acquisition, it's the auditor's 'subjective' flag on the area most at risk.

rfm_tuples.R: 'During 2024, the Company continued to actively market for sale its nine-acre corporate headquarters campus (the Campus) located in Clayton, Missouri. In January 2025, the Company entered into an agreement to sell the main portion of the Campus, subject to certain closing conditions. In February 2025, the Company entered into two letters of intent to sell.' 'if comparable sales prices cannot be secured, we may have to recognize a loss on disposal.'
rfm_tuples.f: Mode-B: real-estate monetization as a liquidity bridge. A company selling its HQ campus while levering up the revolver for acquisition and buybacks is balance-sheet engineering - converting illiquid PP&E to cash to bridge the operating cash flow gap.
rfm_tuples.M_value: 9-acre Clayton MO HQ campus actively marketed throughout 2024; main-portion sale agreement Jan 2025; 2 additional LOIs Feb 2025 - same month as Stuart Weitzman signing. 10-K does NOT disclose expected proceeds or carrying value gap. Risk-factor explicitly contemplates loss-on-disposal. New leased HQ build-out 'could be delayed or cost more than expected.'
rfm_tuples.interpretation: HQ sale + relocation during a year of revolver-funded buyback + debt-funded acquisition is balance-sheet engineering: monetize PP&E to fund discretionary capital actions while operating cash flow shrinks. Undisclosed proceeds figure and explicit loss-on-disposal risk indicate the cash bridge may be smaller than implied. Mode-B catches this as a coordinated cash-management maneuver - taken together with revolver utilization and Stuart Weitzman, suggests management is more constrained than 'compliance with all covenants' framing implies.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Net cash provided by operating activities $104.6 [vs] $200.2 (-$95.6) ... reflecting Lower earnings in 2024 compared to last year, primarily driven by lower consumer demand; An increase in inventory in 2024 compared to a decrease in 2023; A decrease in trade accounts payable in 2024 compared to an increase last year.' Net earnings $106.1M vs $171.8M (-38.2%).
rfm_tuples.f: Earnings-quality check: operating cash flow declined 47.7% while net earnings declined 38.2%, a 9.5pp gap. Inventory build into a weakening comp environment + AP contraction is classic working capital stress. Mode-B: derive cash conversion deterioration trajectory.
rfm_tuples.M_value: FY24: Net earnings $106.1M, OpCFO $104.6M, cash conversion 98.6%. FY23: Net earnings $171.8M, OpCFO $200.2M, cash conversion 116.5%. YoY: -17.9pp in cash conversion. Inventories ($23.3M) WC drain in FY24 vs +$39.5M source in FY23 (a $62.8M swing). Trade AP similar negative swing. Inventories on balance sheet $565.2M - building into negative comp environment.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Cash conversion dropped 17.9pp while narrative still emphasizes strategic-positioning language. Building $23M of incremental inventory into a Q4 comp cliff and a pending tariff regime is exactly the working capital stress that precedes promotional gross margin compression. The 9.5pp earnings-vs-cash-flow gap means reported EPS is being supported by working capital build that will reverse out in FY25 as inventory is marked down (cf. the CAM on markdown reserves).

rfm_tuples.R: '[Brand Portfolio] segment net sales $1,226.0 [vs] $1,270.9 (-$44.9) (-3.5)%.' 'Famous Footwear segment net sales $1,556.5 [vs] $1,609.4 (-$52.9) (-3.3)%.' 'Operating earnings $149.9 [vs] $194.5 (-$44.6) (-22.9)%.' Gross margin 44.9% (vs 44.8%, +6 bps).
rfm_tuples.f: Sector-specific (footwear retail): channel-mix and segment-margin decomposition. Both segments declined ~3.3-3.5% in revenue but operating earnings collapsed -22.9% - implied 6.6x operating deleverage. Mode-B: derive segment-level operating margin compression and forward EBIT risk.
rfm_tuples.M_value: FY24 consolidated revenue -3.4%, operating earnings -22.9% - operating deleverage of ~6.7x. Gross margin essentially flat (+6 bps) - the operating decline is entirely SG&A deleveraging. SG&A ratio rose ~140 bps as wage inflation, marketing spend, and Famous Footwear store-fleet fixed-cost absorption deteriorated against declining traffic. Operating earnings $149.9M is the lowest full-year operating earnings since FY20 pandemic disruption.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: 6.7x operating deleverage on a -3.4% revenue decline tells you the cost structure is rigid (leases, store labor, distribution fixed costs) and incremental revenue softness flows almost entirely through to EBIT. With FY25 facing tariff pass-through pressure on gross margin, Stuart Weitzman integration costs, wage inflation, and HQ relocation costs, operating earnings trajectory points to further EBIT compression. The 'modest gross margin pressure' language is inconsistent with the 6.7x operating deleverage already observed.

supplemental_signals.auditor_history: Ernst & Young LLP since 1917 (108 yrs). Unqualified FY24 opinion. Sole CAM = Brand Portfolio Inventory Markdown Reserves ($550.2M finished goods, only 3.2% reserve).
supplemental_signals.going_concern: None. Liquidity = $29.6M cash + $272.3M revolver availability = $301.9M total. Credit Agreement matures Oct 5, 2026 (17 months post-cutoff).
supplemental_signals.leadership_continuity: CEO John W. Schmidt (since Jan 2023), CFO Jack P. Calandra (since Oct 2022). Both >2 years tenure. Diane Sullivan retained as Executive Chair.
supplemental_signals.capital_action_vs_cashflow: Revolver $219.5M (+20.6% YoY); FY24 buyback $65M explicitly funded by revolver; Stuart Weitzman $105M debt-financed (summer 2025 close); OpCFO $104.6M (-47.7% YoY). Buyback + dividend + acquisition = ~$180M vs $104.6M OpCFO.
supplemental_signals.tariff_exposure: China $244.7M (49.5%); China+Vietnam $454.9M (92%). NO quantitative scenario disclosure. 25% incremental China tariff implies ~$61M COGS pressure = ~40% of FY24 operating earnings.
supplemental_signals.channel_mix_risk: Brand Portfolio $1.226B (45%) wholesale to department stores. Zero quantitative top-customer disclosure. Famous Footwear $1.556B (57%) family-mall retail with declining traffic.
supplemental_signals.comp_evolution: FY23 -6.3% -> FY24 -1.3% (improvement headline). Q3 standalone +2.5%. YTD 39-week -0.9%. Implied Q4 standalone ~-2.5% - Q3 recovery reversed in largest selling quarter.
supplemental_signals.real_estate_monetization: 9-acre Clayton MO HQ campus sale Jan 2025 + 2 LOIs Feb 2025. Proceeds undisclosed. Loss-on-disposal risk explicit.
supplemental_signals.covenant_history: Fourth Amended and Restated Credit Agreement + Sixth Amendment (Apr 2023). Long renegotiation history. Springing FCCR 1.25x if availability falls below greater of $40M / 10% of Loan Cap for 30 days.
supplemental_signals.earnings_quality: Cash conversion 98.6% (FY24) vs 116.5% (FY23). Inventory build $23M into negative comp environment sets up FY25 markdown pressure (per CAM).

summary: CAL shows the classic late-cycle mall-anchored specialty-retailer distress pattern - technically compliant with no going concern but multiple Mode-B disclosure failures and aggressive cycle-bottom capital allocation. Top findings: (1) Q4 Famous Footwear comp cliff (~-2.5% standalone) reversing the Q3 +2.5% recovery narrative - visible only via claim_evolution between FY24 10-K and pre-cutoff Q3 10-Q, not separately quantified in MD&A; (2) Stuart Weitzman $105M debt-funded acquisition layered on a revolver already up 20.6% YoY plus continued buybacks while OpCFO collapsed -47.7% - coordinated lever-up into a deteriorating fundamental environment with a 17-month refinancing wall (Oct 2026 maturity); (3) 92% of sourcing exposed to China+Vietnam tariffs with ZERO quantitative scenario disclosure and qualitative 'well-positioned, modest margin pressure' framing inconsistent with the 6.7x operating deleverage already shown in FY24. Supporting tells: zero quantitative wholesale customer concentration for a $1.226B department-store-channel segment, HQ campus sale as liquidity bridge, EY flagging markdown reserves as sole CAM, revolver-funded buyback. Verdict under honesty-alpha framework: SHORT-tier - disclosures are technically compliant but the narrative pillars (Q3 recovery, 'well-positioned' on tariffs, accretive Stuart Weitzman, healthy capital allocation) do not survive Mode-B reconstruction.
